messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Electrician
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Breathing): Heavy breathing sounds, Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociation: I pretend it happened to someone else, Counterfactual Thinking: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Vignette:
Linh Tran is a 54-year-old Vietnamese American woman who has worked for many years as an electrician, most often on commercial jobs where she moves through half-finished buildings in a hard hat, tool belt on her hips, and the constant noise of drills, fans, and shouted instructions around her. She is divorced and lives alone. When she describes the event that still divides her life into a before and after, she does not begin with one dramatic accident but with the memory of becoming critically ill and suddenly finding herself in a hospital bed, frightened that she might not survive. What remains sharp for her is not a sequence she tells smoothly from start to finish, but flashes anchored in the body: the strain of trying to breathe, the sound of heavy breathing in the room, and the sterile hospital smell that seemed to coat everything. She remembers lying there listening for air, alert to each labored inhale, and thinking with a stark, simple fear that she could die here.

Since that illness, reminders arrive in ways that feel immediate and involuntary. Heavy breathing is one of the strongest. On job sites, if a coworker climbs a ladder carrying conduit and stops beside her breathing hard, Linh’s body tightens before she has formed any thought about why. She has described her reaction as happening “faster than my mind.” Her chest goes rigid, her muscles tense, and she feels a surge through her body as if danger is already present. The smell of antiseptic can do the same thing. Walking past a medical clinic in a strip mall, or catching the sharp clean scent of disinfectant in a workplace restroom, she is abruptly back in the atmosphere of the hospital. The anniversary of the illness brings its own apprehension. As that date approaches each year, she becomes watchful and uneasy, already braced for something she cannot fully name, as though her body is remembering on its own.

When those moments happen, Linh often feels strong physical reactions that she experiences as unmistakable and alarming. She becomes tense and keyed up, and she watches herself for signs that something is wrong. She has come to expect her body to react before she has had time to make sense of what she has encountered, which leaves her feeling as though she can never fully get ahead of it. Even outside obvious reminders, she lives with a near-constant readiness, shoulders held tight and attention pulled toward any bodily shift that might signal danger.

In the months after the illness, Linh found herself dealing with it in ways that felt practical at the time. One was to think about the hospitalization as if it had happened to someone else. When memories pressed in, distancing herself from them gave her a brief sense of space, as though she could step out of the story and avoid the full force of what it meant. She also spent long stretches imagining the life she might have had if the illness had never happened. She would picture a different version of the past and compare it to the one she is living now, dwelling on how much calmer and more straightforward things might have been. These thoughts did not arrive as abstract philosophy; they came while driving home from work, while heating dinner, while sitting alone in the evening with the sense that her life had split onto a path she never chose.

She also began avoiding anything that linked her to medical settings. She postponed physical examinations, put off appointments, and stayed away from hospitals and ambulances whenever she could. If a work assignment was near a hospital renovation or service entrance, she noticed herself becoming guarded before she even got out of the truck. The smell, the sight of medical transport, the suggestion that she might have to enter a clinical space all felt like too much. Over time this avoidance narrowed her world in concrete ways. She became reluctant to attend to her own healthcare, and people around her noticed how firmly she refused anything that might bring her near treatment settings. At work, where electricians are expected to move where the job requires, this created awkward moments when she tried to steer clear of certain locations without wanting to explain why.

By the time Linh came for help, she was tired of living as if her body were always one step away from alarm. What finally pushed her into treatment was not one new crisis but the accumulation of these moments: recoiling at the sound of someone breathing heavily behind her on a job, feeling her whole system surge at the scent of antiseptic, and realizing another anniversary was approaching with the familiar dread already gathering. She is frightened by how quickly her reactions take over and by how much effort goes into staying away from reminders. At the same time, she hopes for something simple and deeply important to her—that she might be able to be around medical settings when necessary, move through work without her body constantly bracing, and think about what happened as something that belongs to her past rather than something she has to keep outrunning.
